definition: A model that describes matter as being made up of tiny particles that are always moving. Used to explain the properties of solids, liquids and gases.
A state of matter where particles are closely packed in a regular arrangement, vibrating in fixed positions. Has a definite shape and volume.
A state of matter where particles are close together but can move past each other. Has a definite volume but takes the shape of its container.
A state of matter where particles are far apart and move randomly at high speed. Has no definite shape or volume.
The change of state from solid to liquid. Occurs at the melting point when particles gain enough energy to break free from their fixed positions.
The change of state from liquid to solid. Particles lose energy and form a fixed regular structure.
The change of state from liquid to gas at the surface of a liquid. Can occur at temperatures below the boiling point.
The change of state from liquid to gas throughout the liquid at a fixed temperature — the boiling point.
The change of state from gas to liquid. Particles lose energy and form a liquid.
The change of state directly from solid to gas without passing through the liquid state.
The energy needed to change the state of a substance without changing its temperature. Supplied or released during a change of state.
The energy needed to change the state of 1 kg of a substance without changing its temperature. Measured in J/kg.
The energy needed to melt (or freeze) 1 kg of a substance at its melting point without changing its temperature.
The energy needed to evaporate (or condense) 1 kg of a substance at its boiling point without changing its temperature.
The mass per unit volume of a substance. ρ = m/V. Measured in kg/m³ or g/cm³.
The amount of matter in an object. Measured in kilograms (kg). Does not change with location.
The amount of space an object occupies. Measured in m³ or cm³.
The energy needed to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a substance by 1°C. Measured in J/kg°C.
The total kinetic and potential energy of all the particles in a substance. Increases when a substance is heated.
A measure of the average kinetic energy of the particles in a substance. Measured in °C or Kelvin (K).
The lowest possible temperature, −273°C or 0 K, at which particles have minimum kinetic energy and gas pressure would be zero.
A temperature scale starting at absolute zero (0 K = −273°C). Used in gas law calculations. K = °C + 273.
The force exerted by gas particles colliding with the walls of their container per unit area. Increases with temperature or decreased volume.
At constant temperature, the pressure of a gas is inversely proportional to its volume. P₁V₁ = P₂V₂.
At constant volume, the pressure of a gas is directly proportional to its absolute temperature (in Kelvin). P/T = constant.
The pressure exerted by the weight of air above a point. Decreases with increasing altitude as there is less air above.
The random movement of small particles (e.g. pollen in water or smoke in air) caused by collisions with faster-moving molecules. Evidence for the particle model.
